claims.text: Applying high-pressure torsion to a eutectic high-entropy alloy will simultaneously increase its strength and ductility.
The target as-processed eutectic high-entropy alloy has a coarse lamellar or dual-phase microstructure.
In-situ ceramic or intermetallic reinforcements elevate the strength of the target alloy.
The target alloy exhibits brittle behavior such as cleavage fracture before HPT.
HPT can be applied as a post-processing treatment to a eutectic high-entropy alloy under a fixed pressure and selected number of revolutions.
Controlled HPT will refine the alloy's grains to the submicron scale.
HPT can retain the eutectic phase distribution without introducing deleterious contaminants.
HPT will produce a uniform ultrafine-grained microstructure.
HPT will homogenize the distribution of the eutectic phases and reduce the size and spacing of brittle constituents.
The HPT-induced grain refinement will increase strength through Hall–Petch dislocation impediment.
A more uniform phase distribution will improve strain partitioning across the composite microstructure.
Improved strain partitioning will alleviate stress concentrations and promote more ductile deformation.
Optimized HPT will increase yield strength by approximately 20–50% relative to the coarse as-cast state.
Optimized HPT will increase total strain to fracture by a percentage similar to or slightly below the predicted strength improvement.
The simultaneous improvement is expected during room-temperature mechanical testing.
Excessive HPT-induced damage, oxidation, or compositional inhomogeneity can prevent the proposed simultaneous improvement.
The balance of strength and ductility improvements depends on alloy composition and HPT pressure, revolution count, and temperature control.
